notes.meaning: The heading gives music directions. No one is sure what "Sheminith" means, though it may point to a low, deep tune that suits a sad song. This is the first of the seven "penitential psalms," which are prayers of sorrow for sin. David knows he deserves correction and does not ask God to stop it. He asks that God correct him like a loving father, not in anger that would crush him.

David begs for mercy. His plea is not that he is good but that he is weak, like a drooping, withered plant. His "bones" stand for his whole body and strength, which are shaken with pain and fear. Only God can heal him, body and soul.

The trouble in David's soul is even worse than the pain in his body. He feels God's love is hidden and fears God's judgment. His cry "How long?" breaks off, as if grief stopped his words. Yet he still turns to God as his only hope.

David feels God has turned His face away, so he asks God to turn back to him. He wants to be received into God's favor again. He bases his plea only on God's "loving devotion," His faithful love, not on anything he has earned. Even someone who has wandered from God may ask Him to return.

"Sheol" is the grave, the place of the dead. David is not denying life after death. He means that if he dies, his chance to praise God here on earth will end. He could no longer thank God before His people or help others know Him. So he asks God to spare him so he can keep serving.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars say the psalm writers pictured only one shadowy place for all the dead, far from God's light. In this view, Christians pray this verse by thinking of hell, where there truly is no praise of God.

notes.meaning: David pictures how deep and how great his grief is. He has groaned until he is worn out, and he weeps so much at night that his bed seems to float in tears. He mourns alone in private, before God. A brave man like David, who faced Goliath, is not made smaller by such tender sorrow over sin.
David's eyes have grown weak and dim from crying, like the eyes of an old man. His enemies make his grief worse. They mock him in his trouble and twist the meaning of his tears.

Suddenly the mood changes. David is sure God has heard him, so he tells the evildoers who mocked him to go away. He also turns his back on sin and on bad company. His tears were a kind of prayer that God heard, even without words. Jesus later uses these same words in judgment (Luke 13:27).

David says again that the LORD has heard his cry. God has heard, so David trusts He will accept his prayer and answer it in His good time. He uses what God has done before as hope for what God will do next.

David's enemies thought he would fall, but now they will be ashamed and troubled instead. Some read this as a prayer that they will be sorry, turn back, and change their ways. Others read it as a warning of what will come on them if they do not turn. Either way, God can rescue His people suddenly.
